provenance: Extended facts read from each answer's text for the Prolog oracle (examples/v40_fatwa_rules.pl); the ruling is the text's own for the case. Facts beyond the encoder's are the ones the tranche's gaps need. null = the text does not settle it, or the ruling does not depend on it.

cases.note: Doubt (shakk) about the number of rakʿas against the presumed lesser count (zann): he builds on certainty
Preponderant belief (ghalabat al-ẓann = zann), aided by the external sign of the people beside him (amara), may override the presumed lesser count (zann)
Presumed purity (zann) vs mere doubt of a wet dream (shakk), no sign seen: no ghusl, ṭawāf valid
Presumed purity of the garment (zann) vs verified urine on it (qat): washing is obligatory
Presumed purity of the garment (zann) vs doubt whether urine splashed (shakk): no washing
Quoted Permanent Committee: presumed wuḍūʾ (zann) vs verified emission of a drop (qat): istinjāʾ and wuḍūʾ required
Quoted Permanent Committee: presumed wuḍūʾ and purity (zann) vs doubt of a drop (shakk): nothing required
Presumed continuing menstruation (zann) vs doubt whether it ended before fajr (shakk): she counts as menstruating, so no fajr make-up and the fast is invalid
Waswās in purity (wahm) against the established state (zann): it is to be ignored
Presumed continuing menstruation (zann) vs complete dryness, one of the two sharʿī signs of purity (qat, amara): ghusl and fast valid
Presumed menstruation (zann) vs bare dryness without the full sign, i.e. no certainty of purity (shakk): the first two fasts must be made up
Established purity (zann) vs ṣufra/kudra actually seen after it (qat that it was seen, amara); text: not menstruation.
Presumed wuḍūʾ (zann) vs doubt of breaking wind (shakk): ignore the doubt
Presumed wuḍūʾ (zann) vs certainty of wind (qat): wuḍūʾ is broken even without sound or smell
Presumed wuḍūʾ (zann) vs gas sounds inside the belly, an external sign (amara) that gives no knowledge of an exit (shakk): wuḍūʾ intact
Ibn Bāz: presumed purity (zann) vs waswās about smells that may come from elsewhere (wahm): complete the prayer
Presumed purity (zann) vs doubt of janāba (shakk), with a possible trace on the clothes that may be old (amara): no ghusl, ṭawāf valid
Presumed purity and no discharge (zann) vs doubt of madhy or manī (shakk
Presumed no discharge (zann) vs certainty that something came out (qat): it is madhy, so purity is lifted
Presumed purity (zann) vs felt wetness (an indicator, amara) of doubtful origin (shakk) after sprinkling water: attribute it to the water
Certain purity, ghusl, ṭawāf, then ṣufra/kudra seen (qat, amara); text: not menstruation, ṭawāf valid.
Presumed purity (zann) vs doubt of nullification during or after ṭawāf (shakk): ṭawāf and prayer valid
Presumed absence of divorce intent (zann) vs doubt about forgotten intent behind kināya words (shakk): no divorce
Presumed continuation of the marriage (zann) vs an unverified recollection that kināya words were used (shakk): they may resume
Before God: presumed marriage and no relapse (zann) vs the wife's own certainty that he relapsed (qat, signs in his conduct): she must act on it
Wife's certainty of relapse (qat, signs in his conduct) vs presumed marriage (zann); in the apparent ruling his denial prevails.
Ibn Qudāma, quoted: presumed marriage (zann) vs a triple divorce established by two upright witnesses (qat): she may not let him approach her
Guest took it without permission or bumped into it: liable; the text does not make it depend on fault.
Family 'erred' (اخطأتم) in bringing a folk healer, but owe no diya because the healer was the direct actor.
Healer liable if the death was caused by him through lack of skill, transgression or negligence (the conditional branch the text rules on).
Dentist's hand erred (drilled too far): liable even if skilled; skill only removes the sin.
Employee driver in an accident where the fault was his: liable for the other car.
Employer who lent the car has no connection to the employee's fault: not liable.
Speeding driver 100% at fault hit a parked car: liable for damage plus loss in value.
Other driver at fault injured the questioner's body or car: owes compensation.
Questioner drove lawfully and only caused the woman to step back: not liable (indirect cause, no transgression).
Other driver struck her directly: liable as direct actor (even without transgression), unless he could not avoid her.
If the questioner was speeding and the other driver did not transgress: questioner liable as a transgressing indirect cause.
Permitted speed, pedestrian crossed suddenly 1-2 m ahead where there is no crossing: no diya, no kaffara.
Driver who could have avoided the collision or was speeding: liable.
Driver and pedestrian both at fault: driver owes kaffara and diya in proportion to his fault.
Questioner slowed down; the tailgater swerved without looking: questioner not liable.
Stubborn tailgater is an indirect cause but transgressed and was negligent: liable, not the overturned driver.
Airline as common hired worker broke a suitcase: liable even without transgression or negligence.
Driver erred (crossed despite other car's right of way) while driving at a friend's request: liable; ignorance of liability no excuse.
Friend who asked him to drive and rode along (even if he misdirected him): not liable; liability on the direct actor.
Driver hit an animal without negligence and could not avoid it: not liable.
Driver hit an animal through negligence: liable.
Pram placed in a rarely used spot, grandmother tripped: not a transgression, not liable.
If she transgressed (e.g. in the walkway): liable for the fracture.
Death a week later: not liable for the life unless doctors attribute it to the fracture; the text leaves the attribution open (liable if attributed).
Reasonable speed, warned the pedestrian, he stepped back suddenly: not liable.
If she sped or failed to try to avoid him: liable for the fracture and the wound.
Even if negligent, not liable for the death: the text attributes it to COVID hypoxia, not the fracture.
Valuable find outside the Haramayn, announced a year, owner unknown: his after the year.
Find in the Haramayn (Mecca and Medina alike here): never owned, announce forever; handing it to the Haramayn authorities is the stated alternative.
Trivial find (rope, sandal strap, small money): no announcement, he may use it; giving it in charity for the owner is also allowed.
Stray camel and animals that fend off small predators may not be picked up.

Wallet found in the Meccan Haram: IslamQA follows the view that it is never owned and is announced forever, or handed to the officials (Ibn ʿUthaymin); the other view owns it after a year (finderOwns).
Watch from the Meccan Haram kept four years unannounced: return it to the Great Court of Mecca for the Haram lost-property committee.
Things people do not pursue (whip, loaf, date, stick): owned by the finder without announcement.
Camels, horses, birds, gazelles and the like: forbidden to pick up, not owned by announcing.
Large self-keeping items (huge pots, timber, iron): forbidden to take like stray camels; not an animal, so the schema has no field for this.

Edible stray animal (sheep, young camel, chicken): do the best for the owner: eat it owing its value, sell it and keep the price, or keep and feed it without owning it. The text does not make it his at once.
Perishable find (melon, fruit): eat it owing its value or sell it and keep the price until the owner comes; perishability has no field here.
Ordinary property (money, vessels): keep it in trust and announce it.
Gold/silver announced a year with no owner: he may spend it (hadith of Zayd b. Khalid), returning it if the owner ever comes.
Stray sheep during the announcement: eat it at an assessed value, sell it and keep the price, or keep it through the announcement period.
Stray sheep whose owner does not come after the announcement period: it belongs to the finder.
Fifty riyals at the Jamarat: too small to announce; charity for the owner is fine, as is handing it to the lost-property officials or announcing it.
cases.oracle_gap: The text permits charity, handing it to the officials, or announcing it, and never says he may keep it, unlike 126502.f001 with the same facts; the facts carry no distinction between the two answers.

cases.note: Ten to fifteen riyals in Mecca: trivial; he may use or eat it; announcing it or giving it in charity is also fine.
Pen on a desk worth up to about fifty riyals: may be taken and used without announcement.
Find of real value: must be announced a year before it is owned.
Buried treasure with pre-Islamic marks is rikaz: a fifth is due.
Treasure buried by Muslims is luqata: announce a full year, then the finder owns it (returning it if the owner appears).
Treasure in bought or gifted land: IslamQA leans (Ibn Qudama, Ibn ʿUthaymin) to the finder keeping it after the fifth; the majority give it to the land's first owner or his heir.
Buried treasure with pre-Islamic marks is rikaz: a fifth is due.
Treasure buried by Muslims is luqata: announce a full year, then the finder owns it (returning it if the owner appears).
Treasure in bought or gifted land: IslamQA leans (Ibn Qudama, Ibn ʿUthaymin) to the finder keeping it after the fifth; the majority give it to the land's first owner or his heir.
Meccan Haram find: IslamQA prefers that it is announced forever and never owned; Hanafis, Malikis, Hanbalis and one Shafiʿi report treat it like other finds (finderOwns).
Money found in the Medina Haram, held three days: keep it and announce it a full year, or hand it to the responsible authorities; not charity yet.
Medina Haram find after a year: like other lands, his after the year (Shafiʿi majority, Ibn ʿUthaymin); al-Bulqini and others: never owned (hold).
iPod announced two months: a trust to be announced a full year; no use meanwhile.
Valuable find announced a year with no owner: his after the year.
Trustee carrier; airport authorities seized the money under currency rules; no fault; not liable. Text does not assess the seizure's lawfulness; an authority acted, so lawful_authority_act=true.
Depositee, deposit perishes without transgression or negligence; not liable.
Depositee who transgresses against the deposit is liable if it perishes.
Depositee negligent in guarding the deposit is liable if it perishes.
Deposited animal dies after the depositee stops feeding it, an omission of a duty (tafrit); liable.
Depositee hands the deposit to his wife/servant/treasurer, as permitted; it perishes without transgression or negligence; not liable.
Entrusted carrier kept the item in a proper hirz, no transgression or negligence, then it was stolen; not liable.
Trustee neglected to keep it in its hirz, then it was stolen; liable.
Trustee transgressed (placed it in an unsafe place, disposed of it or used it), then it was stolen; liable.

Depositee disposed of the deposit without the owner's permission (transgression; text says he is 'in the ruling of the usurper'); part was lost in transfers; liable. hand=wrongdoer would also give true.
Employee diverted lawfully confiscated marble to a relative: usurpation (wrongdoer, transgressed); his act was not the lawful one; liable.
Hypothetical lawful confiscation and destruction as ta'zir bil-mal: 'no blame'. Hand is the authority's agent, closest to trustee.
Trustee of a deposited sorcery book destroys it against the owner's request for return (beyond permission, though the text says shariah requires it); no value, so not liable.
Guest held the furniture with permission and it broke in his hand without error or carelessness: not liable (liable only if he erred or was careless).
Bank as mudarib in an investment account; capital lost without fault; not bound to return it.
Bank as mudarib whose shortcoming (taqsir) caused the loss; liable for capital.
Bank holding current-account deposits = borrower of a loan, hand of guarantee by contract; bound to repay.
Investment account (mudaraba): guarantee removed, bank as trustee with no fault; ruling false (record reclassed segmentation_error).
Seller keeps sold goods the buyer has not collected (not prevented); without transgression or negligence he is not liable.
Same seller-custodian, with transgression; liable.
Same seller-custodian, with negligence; liable.
Seller who prevents the buyer from taking delivery bears the loss 'because he is like the usurper'; hand=wrongdoer.
Bribe paid only to obtain the payer's own right (not an illicit exchange); the known payer gets it back.
Bribe for what was not his right, which he obtained; IslamQA (Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn al-Qayyim) spends it on the poor and public interests, while another group (طائفة) says return it to the owner.
Return owed but the payer and his heirs cannot be found after searching (بعد البحث والتحري); the text never says the search was given up, so despaired is null; charity on his behalf.
Government rest-house services, which are public money; the owner is the state (identified), and the value goes to any public-interest channel or the poor.
cases.oracle_gap: Public money spent on public-interest channels without asking whether the paying body can take it back; with the state as an identifiable owner, the oracle returns it to the owner, as 260724.f001's text does.

cases.note: Earmarked burial donations no longer needed; returned to the known donors (who may then give it to the widow).
Quoted Permanent Committee: treatment money for a patient who died is returned to the known party that gave it.
Donors unknown or unreachable (تعذر), with no despair stated; spent on a similar charitable channel.
She tried every way and finding the owners is 'impossible' (من المستحيل إيجادهم); charity on their behalf.
Quoted Permanent Committee: an owner who turns up after the charity may ratify it, or else is paid his right.
She may give the charity to her own poor family, whose maintenance she does not owe (with Ibn ʿUthaymīn's no-favouritism proviso).
Salary from a state teaching post for days not worked, returned to the paying body where possible.
If return to the state employer is not possible: charity or state-funded public interests; no despair stated.
The widow's inheritance share must be sought out and given to her, or to her heirs if she has died.

If she cannot be reached, the heirs may hold her share for her or give it in charity on her behalf. The text permits both and I recorded the first; no despair is stated for her, though the quoted Ibn Taymiyya ties charity to despair.
cases.oracle_gap: The text permits a choice: hold her share for her or give it in charity on her behalf. A ruling records one option; the oracle gives the charity route (publicInterest).

cases.note: If she appears after the charity she chooses between ratifying it or taking her share.
Stolen goods go back to the owner or his heirs by default; theft is not an exchange.
She does not know her victims after trying to recall them; despair is not stated; she may give charity on their behalf.
